lectures.title: Streamlining Filesystem Structure: the Project usrmerge

cues.en: Let's now have a quick look at the Merge project and what's the reasoning behind it.
And for that, we need to realize that Linux has a long history.
So it all started usually in computers.
We were, for example, using a hard disk drives like spinning disks and they were pretty small.
This one is already a more recent one.
We can see it here at the connector.
The older ones used different connectors there.
But imagine we only had, for example, a 100MB or maybe even just one gigabyte or something like this.
And then we need to be really careful how we allocate this space.
And the Merge project answers the questions why we are nowadays moving certain folders into the user
folder.
But back in the days it was important that those folders were separate folders.
The idea is that we can nowadays simplify the file system hierarchy on Linux systems and we can merge
those folders.
But back then it was extremely important to differentiate between slash lib and slash usr lib.
The reason is that back then we might have wanted to store slash user on a different physical drive.
So the idea is that we had one drive that's responsible for booting up the system and providing all
the essential tools that we would need, for example, if the other drive would break or if some serious
problems happen on our system and everything else, this slash user folder that could be on a secondary
drive and then those two drives could work together.
So back then this was essential because we had this limitations, this limitation that the drives could
be extremely small and we needed to combine those drives or we needed to use a different drive for the
user folder just for storage space reasons.
So slash bin, slash bin and slash lib were meant to contain only applications that are absolutely necessary
to fix a broken system so that we can boot up in a so-called recovery mode.
And then.
For example, access also the other drive if we wanted to, but if that other drive would fail, we
would still have a recovery mode that we could work with.
Nowadays, you can imagine with modern SSDs and enough storage and abundance or really affordable storage,
this is definitely no longer necessary, at least usually.
And thus we are nowadays able to simplify our directory structure.
And because that's a process that takes really, really long because we have programs that should still
be able to run.
This is a process that probably will still take several years or even decades where those previous folders
are still being symlinked to USB bin just so that old software is still compatible with our modern system.
But that's the idea of the USB merge project.
Be aware USB merge is not part of the filesystem hierarchy standard.
Nonetheless, Linux distributions are more and more starting to implement it or implementing it already.
And this is the reasoning or the reason why we can find everything in us.r nowadays.
